strengths: The paper addresses a practical and well-motivated problem (online batch selection for SFT) and clearly articulates three desiderata (D1-D3), with a transparent comparison table (Table 1) situating UDS against prior methods on utility, diversity, external-resource dependence, and training-time overhead.

The method is elegant and lightweight: the nuclear norm of the logits matrix requires no gradient computation or external reference model/validation set, and the Kronecker-factorized SRFT projection (Theorem 3.2) with a FIFO memory buffer is a clean way to make inter-sample diversity scoring memory- and compute-efficient, with a correct reduction to a standard fast JL transform (Appendix C.3).

The empirical evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: four benchmarks spanning knowledge, science QA, math, and code; two backbone models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B); six baselines including the SOTA GREATS and RHO-Loss; results averaged over four seeds with standard deviations; plus throughput measurements showing UDS trains faster than full-dataset SFT while improving accuracy.

Useful supporting analyses: component ablations (Table 4) showing both the nuclear-norm and diversity-distance terms contribute, sensitivity to K (Figure 4), to the trade-off factor alpha (Figure 7), and to projection dimensions and buffer size (Figures 5-6), which also verify that the added overhead is negligible.
An honest limitations section discussing the SVD overhead of the nuclear norm for long sequences and failed attempts at randomized-SVD approximation, plus a clear LLM usage declaration.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for the nuclear norm as an 'optimization utility' score is informal and incomplete. The chain of claims (larger Frobenius norm -> larger logits perturbation delta L -> larger loss reduction) is asserted intuitively rather than derived (Section 3.1, Eq. 7-8), and the empirical support (Figure 2) is a Spearman correlation shown for only one model and one dataset (Qwen-2.5-7B on MMLU). The central claim that nuclear norm predicts loss reduction is thus only weakly evidenced.

The 'intra-sample diversity' interpretation is conceptually questionable: a flat singular spectrum of the logits matrix may simply reflect high predictive entropy/uncertainty rather than semantic richness, and the paper does not disentangle the two. There is also a potential length bias, since the nuclear norm of an N x V matrix scales with sequence length N, and this is never discussed or controlled for.

Tuning protocol raises fairness/validity concerns: the selection ratio K and the trade-off factor alpha are chosen per dataset-model pair (Tables 5-6), and the 'optimal alpha' values appear to be selected by test accuracy, suggesting test-set leakage in the main results. It is unclear whether baselines receive comparable per-dataset hyperparameter tuning, and no results with a single fixed alpha across datasets are reported.

The combination score s_intra + alpha * s_inter mixes quantities on very different scales, with optimal alpha varying across nearly an order of magnitude (1e-3 to 7e-3) across datasets; the method's robustness to this ad hoc linear combination without normalization is not analyzed.

Experiments are limited in scope: only LoRA (rank 8) fine-tuning of 7-8B models on a single RTX 3090, and no comparison with strong offline data-selection baselines (e.g., LESS, importance resampling) that the related-work section discusses; the claimed advantage over full-dataset training is therefore only established within the online-selection family at small scale.

Details relevant to reproducibility are missing: the code availability link in the abstract is truncated/incomplete; the practical implementation of the SVD over a ~512 x 152k logits matrix per sample (which dominates the claimed overhead) is not described; and the theory (Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2) is largely assembled from known results (Horn & Johnson; SRFT/FJLT), so the technical novelty rests mostly on the empirical combination.

Some reported results are surprising and under-discussed, e.g., Random selection outperforming full-dataset training on MMLU for Qwen-2.5-7B (54.26 vs 55.32 is close, but Random reaches 9.29 samples/s vs 2.27), and per-dataset epoch counts differing by 20x (ScienceQA 20 epochs vs 1 elsewhere), which complicates interpretation of throughput comparisons.

strengths: The paper targets a practically relevant problem (online batch selection for LLM SFT) and articulates clear desiderata (D1–D3) that make the comparison of methods systematic, at least nominally.

The method is well-engineered for efficiency: it uses only forward-pass outputs (no per-sample gradients), a FIFO memory buffer for inter-sample diversity, and a factored SRFT projection (Theorem 3.2 / Appendix C.3) that avoids storing an NV × d projection matrix, with a correct reduction to known Kronecker-FJLT results.

The empirical evaluation covers four benchmarks (MMLU, ScienceQA, GSM8K, HumanEval), two backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B), four seeds, plus ablations of both components, sensitivity analyses of α, d1, d2, and M, and a data-scale study (Figure 4).
The limitations section is honest about the SVD overhead of the nuclear norm, and an LLM-usage declaration and detailed hyperparameter tables are provided.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim — that the nuclear norm of the logits matrix indicates optimization utility — is not rigorously established. The argument in Section 3.1 relies on informal assertions ('as the Frobenius norm of the logits increases, the perturbation δL also tends to grow uniformly'), and the only supporting evidence is a within-batch Spearman correlation on a single benchmark/model (Figure 2). This falls short for a paper whose headline contribution is a principled scoring criterion.

A crucial ablation is missing: the paper itself shows the nuclear norm and Frobenius norm bound each other, so it is unclear whether the nuclear norm adds anything over simply using ∥L∥_F (or logit magnitude/entropy). Without this control, the claimed 'intra-sample diversity' signal may be a proxy for confidence, and the framing overstates the novelty.

The intra-sample diversity story is internally inconsistent: by the paper's own Table 2, 'Too Hard' samples should be avoided, yet high nuclear norm is claimed to indicate both higher loss reduction and higher token diversity — two properties whose joint relationship to utility is never disentangled.

Potential test-set tuning: the selection ratios (Table 5) and trade-off factors α (Table 6) are reported per dataset/backbone as 'optimal' values without stating what data they were tuned on. Since all methods are evaluated on the same test benchmarks used to pick these hyperparameters, the comparisons against baselines may be unfairly favorable to UDS.

The efficiency claim is narrower than presented. Throughput is only compared against full-dataset training; e.g., Random selection achieves 9.29 samples/s vs. UDS's 3.41 on Qwen/MMLU with nearly comparable accuracy, which undercuts the 'best trade-off' narrative. Additionally, computing the nuclear norm requires an SVD of an N×V matrix (up to ~512×150k) per sample per iteration — the admitted overhead could be substantial, and no wall-clock breakdown isolating this cost is provided.

Theoretical novelty is limited: Lemma 3.1 is a textbook norm inequality, and Theorem 3.2 is a direct application of known Kronecker-FJLT results (Jin et al., 2021; Ailon & Chazelle, 2006); the JL guarantee also involves a polylog(n) factor whose practical implications for the buffer-size regime are not analyzed.

The desiderata table (Table 1) is self-serving: the criteria are defined post hoc around the proposed method, and several checkmarks (e.g., MaxLoss lacking 'intra-sample diversity') are asserted rather than demonstrated.

Some reported gains are small relative to variance (e.g., GSM8K on Llama-3.1-8B: 58.98 vs. 57.03 for GREATS, with ±0.24 vs. ±0.33), and no statistical significance testing is provided. Reproducibility is further weakened by an apparently truncated/broken code availability statement in the abstract.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem (online batch selection for SFT) and the proposed UDS method is well-motivated: it operates purely on forward-pass logits, requires no reference model or validation set, and maintains a lightweight memory buffer, directly addressing real deployment constraints (D1–D3 in Table 1).

The technical framing is reasonably rigorous: the nuclear norm is motivated via a first-order Taylor analysis relating logits magnitude to attainable loss reduction (Eq. 5–8), and the structured bilinear projection is shown (Theorem 3.2 / Appendix C.3) to reduce algebraically to an SRFT with a Johnson–Lindenstrauss distance-preservation guarantee, which gives the inter-sample diversity score a principled basis.

Experiments are broad for this scale: four benchmarks spanning knowledge, QA, math, and code, two backbone models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B), comparisons against relevant baselines including RHO-Loss and the SOTA GREATS, component ablations (Table 4), selection-fraction sweeps (Figure 4), and sensitivity analyses of the key hyperparameters α, d1, d2, and buffer size M with both accuracy and memory/time overhead reported.

Reproducibility is supported: code is released, full training hyperparameters (Tables 8–9), data selection fractions (Table 5), and dataset details (Table 7) are provided; the paper also includes an honest limitations section (SVD overhead for long sequences) and an LLM-usage declaration.
The ablations show that both components individually and jointly improve over random selection, supporting the design rather than attributing all gains to a single trick.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim that the nuclear norm indicates 'intra-sample diversity' is informal and potentially confounded. Lemma 3.1 only bounds the nuclear norm between rank-1 and flat-spectrum extremes; in practice the nuclear norm is dominated by logits magnitude, and the argument that larger nuclear norm implies richer token-level diversity is a heuristic narrative (Figure 3 is an illustrative toy example, not evidence). The utility argument similarly relies on the assertion that δL 'tends to grow uniformly' with logit magnitude, which is not rigorously established.

The empirical correlation between −δℓ and the nuclear norm (Figure 2) is shown for only one model (Qwen-2.5-7B) on one dataset (MMLU); given this correlation is the foundation of the intra-sample score, it should be verified across all benchmarks/backbones.

Hyperparameter tuning raises fairness and potential test-set leakage concerns: the optimal trade-off α and the data selection fraction differ per dataset–model pair (Tables 5–6), and Figure 4 shows UDS's best result is its peak over K. If these were tuned by observing final test accuracy, UDS is effectively validated on the test distribution while the comparison to baselines (which also select the same fraction, but with which tuning budget?) is not clearly equivalent.

Gains over the strongest baseline (GREATS) are modest on several benchmarks (e.g., 95.19 vs 94.17 on ScienceQA, 79.91 vs 78.61 on GSM8K with Qwen-2.5-7B), and are reported with only four seeds on a single GPU setup; statistical significance of the improvements is not tested.

Scale and generality are limited: all experiments use LoRA (rank 8) with batch size 8 on consumer hardware; whether the findings transfer to full fine-tuning, larger models, longer sequences (where the SVD cost the authors themselves flag becomes significant), or multi-GPU settings is untested. Table 1's claim of 'training time reduction' is supported only by modest throughput gains (e.g., 3.41 vs 2.27 samples/s on MMLU/Qwen).

Table 1 is a self-defined desiderata comparison that conveniently marks UDS as satisfying every criterion while baselines fail several; some entries are contestable (e.g., RHO-Loss and GREATS marked as not supporting training-time reduction based partly on implementation/hardware choices), and no diversity-aware offline selection baselines (deduplication, coreset methods) are compared against.

There are presentation lapses: typos ('optimze', 'the LLM extract logits', 'florid', 'Intuitively, A larger'), and the narrative around 'exploitation and exploration' is asserted but not analyzed (no analysis of what kinds of samples UDS selects over training).

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the three desiderata (D1-D3) and the comparison table (Table 1) cleanly position UDS relative to prior online batch selection methods, and the paper clearly identifies concrete gaps (external resources like reference models/validation sets, and computational overhead exceeding full-data training).

The method is genuinely lightweight and self-contained: it reuses forward-pass logits, avoids backpropagation for scoring, and the SRFT-based bidirectional random projection (Theorem 3.2) is a clean and correct way to compress N x V logit matrices into small embeddings while preserving pairwise distances via the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: two backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B), four benchmarks spanning knowledge, science, math, and code, plus substantial appendix experiments (larger batch size B=16, full-parameter fine-tuning, instruction-tuned models, long-context MATH, OOD evaluation on MATH500/AMC23, and comparison with an offline method FisherSFT). Results are consistent across settings.

Ablations and sensitivity analyses are thorough: component-wise ablation (Table 4) shows both nuclear-norm and diversity-distance terms contribute, and Appendix B examines buffer update policies, distance aggregation strategies, random projection constructions, and hyperparameters (d1, d2, M, alpha).

Honest limitations section acknowledges the non-negligible SVD cost of the nuclear norm for long sequences/large vocabularies and the lack of a rigorous proof for the utility correlation; code availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central theoretical link between the nuclear norm of the logits matrix and optimization utility is heuristic. Equations (7)-(8) argue that loss reduction grows in tandem with ||L||_F, and the supporting evidence is only empirical Spearman correlations (Figures 2, 3, 9) computed within batches of size B=8, which is a very small sample for rank correlation and noisy (the fluctuating correlation trajectories and sporadic p-values reflect this). The paper itself concedes no rigorous proof exists.

The 'no external resources / plug-and-play' claim (D2) is weakened by the trade-off factor alpha: Table 6 shows the optimal alpha varies across datasets and backbones by roughly an order of magnitude, so practitioners need per-dataset tuning (extra runs or a validation signal) to obtain the reported results. The sensitivity analysis in Figure 8 is only for Qwen2.5-7B.

The nuclear norm score is scale-dependent (it grows with logit magnitudes, which change over training and differ across datasets), and the linear combination s_intra + alpha*s_inter mixes quantities on different scales without normalization; this makes the method sensitive to training dynamics in ways the paper does not analyze.

Efficiency gains over full-dataset training are modest (e.g., 3.41 vs 3.27 samples/s on MMLU for Qwen2.5-7B; 6.81 vs 6.24 on HumanEval), so the headline 'faster than full SFT' is only marginally supported at the reported selection fractions; also, the diversity-distance computation and SVD overhead are only characterized for max sequence length 512.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (GREATS) are meaningful on MMLU but modest elsewhere (e.g., +1.02 on ScienceQA, +1.30 on GSM8K, +1.24 on HumanEval for Qwen2.5-7B), and no statistical significance tests are reported despite the standard deviations being of comparable magnitude for some benchmarks.

The inter-sample diversity mechanism (average Euclidean distance to a FIFO buffer of recent samples) is fairly standard; the main novelty is the nuclear-norm-as-utility-diversity heuristic, which is interesting but incremental, and the paper does not compare against simpler diversity proxies (e.g., hidden-state embeddings) that could achieve similar effects.

Minor presentation issues: Table 5 refers to selection fractions for CodeAlpaca while main results report HumanEval; the intra-sample diversity interpretation (Figure 4) is illustrated only schematically without quantitative examples; and the rank-based diversity argument relies on the Frobenius norm being fixed, which is not enforced in practice.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four benchmarks (MMLU, ScienceQA, GSM8K, HumanEval), two backbones, plus appendix experiments covering full-parameter fine-tuning, larger batch sizes, instruction-tuned models, long-context (MATH with 2048 tokens), OOD evaluation, and comparison to an offline method (FisherSFT).

Extensive ablation studies (buffer update policies, distance aggregation, random projection constructions, trade-off factor α, projected dimensions, buffer size M) that probe design choices beyond the minimum.

The method is lightweight and self-contained: scoring uses only forward-pass logits, requires no reference model or validation set, and the SRFT-style Kronecker projection (Theorem 3.2, Appendix C.3) is a clean, correct way to avoid storing an NV×d projection matrix.
Honest limitations section acknowledging SVD overhead and the lack of a rigorous proof for the utility correlation, plus an explicit LLM-usage declaration.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are heuristic and only weakly supported. The argument that nuclear norm correlates with loss reduction rests on informal assertions ('δL also tends to grow uniformly', Appendix-style reasoning that conflates logit scale with optimization utility), and the claimed link between nuclear norm and 'intra-sample diversity' is largely definitional (the rank correlation in Figure 3 is close to tautological given the norm bounds). Empirical evidence is a single model/dataset (Qwen-2.5-7B on MMLU).

Hyperparameter and tuning protocol raises fairness and validity concerns: the data selection fraction (Table 5) and trade-off factor α (Table 6) are tuned per model–dataset combination with α values spanning an order of magnitude, and the α sensitivity (Figure 8) shows large swings. It is unclear what data α and the selection fraction were tuned on; if tuned against test accuracy, the headline numbers are optimistically biased.

Results are uneven and fragile-looking: the +8 point jump over Regular on MMLU (55.32→63.34 with only 12.5% of data) is an outlier relative to ~1-point gains on ScienceQA and GSM8K and ~1.3 on HumanEval, and some margins are within reported seed variability (e.g., HumanEval 46.28±0.35 vs 45.04±0.59) with no significance testing.

The JL-style guarantee (Theorem 3.2) requires d ≳ Cε⁻²log(NV)polylog(n), but the empirical configuration (d1=128 for V~150k, N=512) is far from the regime where the bound is meaningful; the theory is thus decorative rather than explanatory for the actual setting.

Table 1 is a self-serving checklist against desiderata the authors themselves define, and the baselines it dismisses (MaxLoss, MaxGrad, RHO-Loss) are configured under potentially unfavorable conditions (e.g., mismatched reference models for RHO-Loss acknowledged in Appendix D.2).
Presentation issues: typos ('optimze', 'the LLM extract logits', 'florid', 'before gradually declines'), inconsistent notation in Eq. (3), and redundant references (Ailon & Chazelle cited twice).

Novelty is modest: the contribution is essentially (i) a norm-based utility proxy from logits plus (ii) a standard embedding-similarity buffer for diversity, with JL sketching as the main technical ingredient; the combination is reasonable but incremental relative to GREATS and prior utility-plus-diversity selection work.

Scale of validation is limited to 7–8B models with LoRA rank 8 in the main results; throughput claims ('faster than full-dataset training') are modest (3.41 vs 2.27 samples/s on one setting) and only partially support the efficiency narrative.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the paper clearly articulates three desiderata (D1–D3) for online batch selection and positions UDS against existing methods in a transparent comparison table (Table 1).

The method is practical and self-contained: it requires no reference model or validation set, operates on forward-pass logits only, and the SRFT-style Kronecker projection (Theorem 3.2) is an elegant way to make inter-sample diversity scoring memory- and compute-efficient with a genuine JL guarantee.

Unusually thorough empirical evaluation: two backbones (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B) across four diverse benchmarks with multiple seeds, plus extensive appendix experiments covering full fine-tuning (Table 11), instruction-tuned models (Table 12), larger batch sizes (Table 10), long-context reasoning (Table 13), OOD evaluation (Table 14), and an offline-selection comparison (Table 15).

Comprehensive ablations: components (Table 4), buffer update policies, distance aggregation, and random projection constructions (Tables 7–9), and sensitivity analyses for d1, d2, M, and α (Figures 6–8).
Honest limitations section that acknowledges the SVD overhead of the nuclear norm and the absence of a rigorous theoretical justification for the utility correlation.
weaknesses: The central claim that the nuclear norm jointly captures 'utility' and 'intra-sample diversity' is only heuristically supported. Figure 9 shows the Frobenius norm correlates with loss reduction almost as strongly as the nuclear norm, so the utility signal may largely reduce to 'large logits are important.' The distinguishing diversity interpretation rests on a generic linear-algebra lemma (Lemma 3.1) plus an empirical rank correlation, yet Table 4 lacks the most informative ablation: a Frobenius-norm-only baseline. Without it, the added value of the nuclear norm over a much simpler statistic is unclear.

The theoretical development (Eqs. 5–8) is loose: the argument that loss reduction 'typically grows in tandem' with the nuclear norm is an informal chain of approximations, and the authors themselves concede no rigorous proof exists. The Adam extension (Appendix C.2) is stated but not analyzed.

Hyperparameter treatment raises fairness and soundness concerns. The trade-off factor α is tuned per dataset and backbone and varies by nearly an order of magnitude (Table 6), and data selection fractions also differ per dataset (Table 5). It is not stated how these were chosen; if tuned on evaluation performance, this gives UDS an advantage the baselines may not enjoy, and it also weakens the plug-and-play claim.

Scale of evaluation is modest: LoRA rank 8, ≤8B models, single RTX 3090, and relatively small training sets. The claims about efficiency and convergence relative to full SFT may not transfer to larger-scale training where the SVD cost of an N×V logits matrix (acknowledged in the limitations) becomes more burdensome.

The inter-sample diversity signal uses only representations of selected samples in a FIFO buffer; distance to recently selected (i.e., already-trained) samples is a proxy for global diversity that could interact with selection dynamics in unstated ways, and the correlation evidence is confined to one model/dataset pair (Qwen-2.5-7B on MMLU).

The desiderata framing in Table 1 is somewhat self-serving (criteria chosen to match the proposed method), and the empirical gains, while consistent, are moderate in absolute terms on several benchmarks.
